content.text:
Updated Ubuntu CI to use `-march=x86-64-v3` for candidate and baseline builds. This retains AVX2; `x86-64-v4` enables AVX-512, beyond [Valgrind’s supported instructions](https://valgrind.org/info/platforms.html).

Verified flag propagation, the local `native` fallback, shell syntax, and diff checks. Full CI hasn’t run locally.

The dependencies also need to be compilied without avx512 for valgrind. Valgrind has an issue where it does not support AVX512 instruction sets. If your CPU supports AVX512, you will need to disable it when compiling Gkeyll. Valgrind does not work with a GPU build and you need a CPU build.

A few modifications must be made.

First, in install-deps/build-openblas.sh change these lines

make USE_OPENMP=0 NUM_THREADS=1 NO_FORTRAN=1 NO_AVX512=1 -j 32
make USE_OPENMP=0 NUM_THREADS=1 NO_FORTRAN=1 NO_AVX512=1 install PREFIX=$PREFIX -j 32
Now re-run mkdeps.sh to rebuild OpenBLAS

Second, within config.mak, set the march to “skylake”, which disables AVX512

Third, inside the makefile, make sure that the march is skylake and add the following options

CFLAGS ?= -mno-avx -mno-avx2 -mno-avx512f

I’ll trace the dependency build and apply the CPU flags throughout Ubuntu CI, including disabling AVX-512 in OpenBLAS. I’m using the compiling and testing skills to check how those settings reach the build.

content.text:
OpenBLAS detects the host CPU independently, so the Gkeyll flag alone is insufficient. I’ll add `NO_AVX512=1` to both OpenBLAS make commands and set Ubuntu CI to `-march=skylake -mno-avx -mno-avx2 -mno-avx512f`. Passing these through `ARCH_FLAGS` writes them into `config.mak` and applies them alongside the Makefile’s existing flags.

I’ll also rebuild OpenBLAS in a temporary prefix and run a focused Valgrind check.
